title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 38
paragraphs: Then as he was leading his army out on its march, Pythius the Lydian, alarmed by the heavenly sign and emboldened by the gifts he had received, came to Xerxes and said: “Master, I would like to ask you for a certain thing, which as it happens is an easy thing for you to grant but a great thing for me if I obtain it.” Xerxes, thinking that the request would be for anything rather than what it actually was, said he would grant it, and bade him speak out and say what he wanted. Pythius, encouraged by this, said: “Master, I have, as it happens, five sons, and it is their lot to be going with you on the march against Greece — all of them. Have pity on me, O king, seeing that I have come to so great an age, and release one of my sons from serving on the campaign, the eldest, so that he may take care of me and of my wealth. The other four take with you, and after you have accomplished what you have in mind, may you have a safe return home.”

Xerxes was furiously angry and answered: “Wretched man, do you dare — when I myself am marching against Greece, taking my sons and brothers and kinsmen and friends — do you dare mention so much as a son of your own, seeing that you are my slave, who ought to be following me in person with your whole household and your wife as well? Know then this: the passionate spirit of a man dwells within his ears; when it has heard good things, it fills the body with delight; when it has heard the opposite, it swells up with rage. Just as you cannot boast of having outdone the king in benefits before, when you did us good deeds and offered to do still more of the same kind, so now, since you have turned to shamelessness, you shall receive not what you deserve but less than you deserve. Your gifts of hospitality shall save from death yourself and four of your sons; but you shall pay the penalty with the life of the one to whom you cling most.” Having so answered, he at once ordered those whose task it was to find the eldest of Pythius's sons and cut him in two in the middle; and when they had cut him, to place the halves one on the right of the road and the other on the left, so that the army should pass between them on its way.
